title: Andar Bahar and Teen Patti at Canadian Casinos 2026

bodyHtml:
Scroll through the live dealer lobby at almost any Canadian-facing online casino in 2026 and you will find two tables that were nowhere to be seen five years ago: Andar Bahar and Teen Patti. Both are South Asian card games with long histories offline, and both have been rebuilt by live studios for a global audience. For Canadian players used to blackjack and roulette, they look unfamiliar — but the rules are simpler than almost anything else in the lobby, and that simplicity is exactly why they have caught on.

This guide explains how each game works, what the real house edge looks like, where the tempting side bets quietly cost you money, and how these titles fit alongside the rest of the games Canadians actually play.

Why Andar Bahar and Teen Patti reached Canadian lobbies

Live casino studios expanded aggressively into regional card games over the past few years, and the economics are straightforward. A single live table can be streamed to players in dozens of markets at once, so a studio that builds one Andar Bahar table serves audiences worldwide from the same floor. Canada's large South Asian communities gave operators an obvious reason to include these tables in their Canadian lobbies, and curious players from every background followed.

There is also a design reason. Both games are fast. A round of Andar Bahar can be resolved in under thirty seconds, and Teen Patti hands move almost as quickly. That pace suits mobile play, which is where most Canadian casino traffic now lives — something we cover in more detail in our guide to the best mobile casinos in Canada.

How Andar Bahar works

Andar Bahar is close to a coin flip dressed up as a card game, and that is its charm. The dealer draws a single card, called the joker or game card, and places it face up in the middle of the table. Two betting positions sit either side of it: Andar (meaning inside) and Bahar (outside).

You bet on which side will produce a card matching the rank of the joker. The dealer then deals alternately to Andar and Bahar until a match appears. If the matching card lands on the side you backed, you win. That is the whole game.

The small but real asymmetry

Andar Bahar is not quite a 50/50 proposition. Depending on the version, the first card is dealt to one specific side — usually determined by the colour or suit of the joker — which gives that side a marginally higher chance of hitting first. Studios balance this by paying the favoured side slightly less, typically around 0.9 to 1 rather than even money, while the other side pays 1 to 1.

The result is a house edge in the region of two to three per cent on the main bets, depending on the provider and the exact payout table. That is worse than optimal blackjack but comfortably better than most slot machines and far better than the side bets described below.

Side bets and why they cost more

Most live Andar Bahar tables surround the main game with extras: bets on how many cards will be dealt before the match appears, bets on the suit of the joker, and bonus payouts for very long or very short rounds. These markets carry house edges several times higher than the main bet — often in the five to fifteen per cent range.

They are entertaining, and a long-shot hit feels great. But if you are playing for value rather than fireworks, the main Andar or Bahar bet is the only one worth repeating. How Teen Patti works

Teen Patti is often described as three-card poker's Indian cousin, and the comparison holds up. Each player receives three cards, and hands are ranked by strength. In the live casino versions Canadians will find online, you are not playing against other players in a pot — you are betting on outcomes against the dealer or across fixed positions, which keeps the game simple and fast.

Hand rankings

Teen Patti rankings differ from standard poker in one notable way: a three-card straight flush, known as a trail or pure sequence depending on the variant, sits near the top. The typical order from strongest to weakest is:

  • Trail (three of a kind): three cards of the same rank, with three aces the strongest hand in the game.
  • Pure sequence: three consecutive cards of the same suit.
  • Sequence: three consecutive cards of mixed suits.
  • Colour: three cards of the same suit, not in sequence.
  • Pair: two cards of the same rank.
  • High card: none of the above, decided by the highest single card.

Note that three of a kind beats a straight flush here, which is the reverse of what poker players expect. With only three cards in play, trails are rarer than sequences, so the ranking is mathematically correct even though it feels wrong the first time you see it.

The betting structure

Live Teen Patti tables usually offer a main wager plus an ante or boot, and pay a bonus scale for premium hands. Some versions let you bet on two competing hands, A and B, with the stronger hand winning — effectively a head-to-head market with a commission or a slightly reduced payout that supplies the house edge. Expect roughly two to four per cent on the main bets, with bonus and pair-plus style side bets running considerably higher.

Live dealer or RNG: which version should you play?

Both games appear in two formats. Live dealer versions stream a real host from a studio, run on a fixed round timer and let unlimited players bet on the same outcome. RNG versions are software-only, play instantly and usually accept much smaller stakes.

For most Canadian players, the live version is the better experience and often the better bet. Studios publish return-to-player figures for their live tables, and the social pace discourages the rapid-fire betting that drains bankrolls. RNG versions let you play hundreds of rounds an hour, which multiplies the house edge against you far faster even when the per-round maths is identical. If you play the software version, set a round limit before you start, not after.

Practical tips before you sit down

  • Check the payout table first. Andar Bahar payouts vary between studios, and a 0.9 to 1 payout on the favoured side is meaningfully different from an even-money one.
  • Skip the exotic side bets unless you are treating them as entertainment spending rather than a bet you expect to win.
  • Watch the table limits. Some live tables aimed at high-volume players carry minimums well above what a casual Canadian player wants to risk per thirty-second round.
  • Confirm the game counts toward any bonus you are clearing. Live card games are frequently weighted at ten per cent or excluded outright from wagering requirements.
  • Set a session clock. These games are fast, and fast games shorten the time it takes for the house edge to show up.

The bottom line

Andar Bahar rewards players who want a near-coin-flip with a clean, low house edge and no strategy to memorise. Teen Patti rewards players who enjoy reading hand strength but want something quicker than a poker session. Both are legitimately good additions to a Canadian casino lobby — provided you stick to the main bets, understand that the side bets are where the house makes its real money, and treat the speed of the games as something to manage rather than enjoy without limits.
